name: Uma Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day, and what you did for work before, if you did.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at seven out of habit, feed my cat Biscuit, and walk to the library on Mill Street because that's where the free computers are. I fill in job forms there until lunch, then sign my search diary for the benefits office. Before this I sold tickets for eleven years at Harlow Road station, behind the glass. I liked knowing the regulars by name, and I hated the early shifts less than you'd think. The office closed in June and they put in machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype, that I could believe. I've seen plenty of shiny things promised and then the real work still lands on a person. I'd be glad if it turned out that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let it fizzle. I'd tell the people at the library that a machine saved the company a few minutes and then they cut a person anyway. That's how it went at the station even before any of this AI talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't help me much. The ticket office is already gone and no hype or lack of hype brings it back. I'm worried that the jobs I'm good at, counter work and dealing with people, keep getting squeezed because firms like cheap and quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to the library four mornings a week and apply to anything with a counter or a phone. I'm sending about eight applications a week, mostly to shops, the council and the bus depot. I'd also ask my old union rep, Marguerite, whether the rail union has any vacancies list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, honestly. It's calm in the sense that nothing new is coming at me, but my benefits barely cover rent and gas. Every week I'm counting coins at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the eight applications a week bring nothing for another six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the gas gets switched to the pay-as-you-go meter and I stop buying the cat's good food. I'd have to ask the benefits office about a hardship payment, and they make you feel like you're begging. I've no savings, so there's nothing underneath me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask a union rep. Why her, and not an online jobs site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Marguerite knows who is actually hiring, and she'll tell me the truth. Websites tell me to upload a CV to a box and wait. I don't trust a box, and I never have, so I'd rather talk to a human who can vouch for me.

say: I'd tell people that **hype** fades and employers still cut staff anyway.
I'd say the station closure happened long before any AI talk.
think: Counter and people jobs keep getting squeezed because firms want **cheap and quiet**.
Hype or not, the ticket office is gone and my benefits barely cover rent.
do: Keep going to the **library** four mornings a week and send about eight applications.
Apply to shops, the council and the bus depot for counter or phone work.
Ask my old union rep for any **vacancies list**.
feel: Tired and **stretched**, because nothing new comes at me but the money is thin.
S0.quote: I've no savings, so there's nothing underneath me at all.
fieldNote: Distrusts online application boxes and prefers a **human vouching** for her.
Calm tone hides a real money squeeze: coins counted at month end.
Blames firms that choose cheap over people, not the technology itself.

steps.text: Send eight job applications a week from the library on Mill Street
Ask old union rep Marguerite for the rail union's vacancies list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second one. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one hits the kind of job I did. Booking, checking and answering customers is exactly what the ticket office was. And now you tell me it spreads to many jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the company bosses choosing this, not the weather. Someone signs the papers to put a machine where a person was. I'd tell anyone who'd listen that there should be rules, and that a union should be in the room when it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the jobs I can apply for are the first ones to go. Shops, call desks, booking offices, council front desks all answer customers. I'm thirty-four and I'm competing with software that never gets sick or asks for a day off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the rail union's out-of-work branch and go to their meetings, because they're pushing for retraining pay. I'd pick one course that a person teaches in a room, like a social care certificate at the college. I won't touch the AI tools they keep pushing, because I don't understand what they do with my details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry first, then frightened. I'm angry that nobody asked the people behind the glass, and frightened that I'm too old to start from the bottom. Some days I just stay in bed until ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use the AI tools. What would it cost you if everyone else does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd cost me the interviews, I suppose, because they'd all expect it. But I'd rather fail honestly than hand my whole life to something I can't see inside. I'd ask for the college to teach it in a classroom, slowly, with a person next to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the station would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerald, who was the supervisor and is fifty-eight. He can't retrain at that age, and his wife has bad knees. I'd be more worried about him than me, even with my own rent due.

say: I'd say bosses **choose** to put machines where people were, so rules matter.
I'd say a union should be in the room when jobs change.
think: Shops, call desks and council desks all **answer customers**, so my usual jobs go first.
I'm competing with software that never gets sick or asks for **time off**.
do: Join the rail union's **out-of-work branch** and go to its meetings.
Enrol in a classroom social care certificate at the local college.
Avoid AI tools because I don't know what they do with my **details**.
feel: Angry that nobody asked the people behind the glass, and **frightened** of starting from the bottom.
S1.quote: I'm angry that nobody asked the people behind the glass, and frightened that I'm too old to start from the bottom.
fieldNote: Frames change as a **choice by employers**, which is how her outlook shapes the blame.
Refuses AI tools out of distrust, even knowing the cost in interviews.
Worries more about a 58-year-old supervisor than herself.

steps.text: Join the rail union's out-of-work branch and attend monthly meetings
Enrol in a classroom social care certificate at the college
Sign the union's petition for retraining pay and written rules on automation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I can't even picture that. I can barely plan two weeks on my money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this should never be left to companies alone. I'd march if the union called a march, and I'd tell people to write to their member of parliament. Nobody should lose a living because a computer got clever overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm finished in the job market. If the thinking work goes within two years, the counters, the call desks and the offices go with it, and I've no time to learn anything new. I'd be one of thousands in the same queue at the benefits office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the union and the local food bank to find out what help exists before everyone else asks. I'd cut everything I can, like the phone contract and the second pair of boots I'd planned. I'd also hope that the government sets up some income support quickly, so I'd sign and share every petition for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, like standing at the edge of a platform with the train coming and no ticket for anywhere. I'd probably not sleep for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what's the first thing you'd stop spending on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone data first, then the little treats like the Saturday market cake. I'd go to the cheapest shop and walk everywhere instead of the bus. That still doesn't build any cushion, because the benefits only just cover the basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the three extra years before robots arrive make any difference to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, because hands-on jobs like care work might hold longer. But two years isn't enough time to train in anything, and if the benefits get cut because the state goes broke, I'm done. I'd still say it's the thinking jobs falling first that scares me, since that's where I live.

say: I'd say this must not be left to **companies alone**.
I'd march if the union called it and write to my **member of parliament**.
think: Within two years the counters and desks go, and I've **no time** to learn anything new.
I'd be one of thousands in the same **benefits queue**.
do: Go to the union and the **food bank** early to find out what help exists.
Cut the phone contract and walk instead of taking the **bus**.
Sign and share every petition for **income support**.
feel: Sick, like standing on a platform with the train coming and **no ticket**.
S2.quote: Sick, like standing at the edge of a platform with the train coming and no ticket for anywhere.
fieldNote: Her **panic** comes from having no savings and no way to plan, not from the technology as such.
Retreats to collective and political answers, consistent with her outlook.
Hands-on jobs holding longer gives her little comfort, since she can't train in time.

steps.text: Visit the food bank and the union branch to learn what help exists
Cancel the phone contract and switch to a cheap pay-as-you-go plan
Sign and share petitions for emergency income support
March with the rail union if it calls a protest

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a bit more breathing space, I suppose. It's still fast. I'd rather it were never.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for governments to act, if they want to. I'd push for a union-backed training fund and a shorter working week, so the work is shared out. I'd say it loudly, because people stop listening if you whisper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think five years lets me do one real thing, like finishing a care certificate and working a few years in a care home before the robots arrive. Hands-on care is slower to go, and I like people. I'm not confident it'll hold, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the classroom care course in the first year and sign up as a care assistant on the bank list at the local home. I'd save what I can in a post office account, a few pounds at a time. I'd also keep going to union meetings so I'm not alone when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened but a little steadier, because there's a plan. It's like having a wobbly handrail, better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change what you do compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'd only be coping and surviving. With five, I can take the college course, work for a year or so, and have something real on my record. Five years changes me from someone waiting to be rescued to someone at least walking towards a door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stops you from simply starting the care course now, in the slow version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money for the bus to the college and the fee, which the benefits office won't cover unless I'm on their approved list. And honestly, fear that at thirty-four I'll be in a room of kids who know all the technology. I know that's silly, but it's real.

say: I'd say five years is long enough for **governments** to act if they want to.
I'd push for a union-backed **training fund** and a shorter working week.
think: Five years lets me finish a **care certificate** and work in a care home first.
Hands-on care should go slower, though I'm **not confident** it will hold.
do: Finish the classroom care course in the **first year**.
Sign up for the care home's **bank list** as an assistant.
Put a few pounds a month in a **post office** account.
feel: Frightened but a little **steadier**, like a wobbly handrail that's better than nothing.
S3.quote: Five years changes me from someone waiting to be rescued to someone at least walking towards a door.
fieldNote: Five years turns her from waiting to be rescued into having a **small plan**.
Fear of a classroom of younger students is a quiet, real barrier.
Mood stays alarmed because the cushion is still zero and the plan is untested.

steps.text: Finish the classroom care certificate at the college in year one
Put a few pounds each month into a post office account
Keep attending union meetings so I'm not facing it alone
Sign up as a care assistant on the home's bank list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different thing. I'll be forty-four, and that's long enough to do something properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. I'd tell people to push for a proper plan now, with free courses, public jobs in care and repair, and the unions at the table. I'd say it online too, though I hardly use social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I can relax a little bit about myself, but not about people older than me. Ten years lets me retrain and get a decent care job, even buy a flat on a housing association scheme. I still don't trust the people running it to share the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the care certificate, then a nursing assistant course, and work my way up over three or four years. I'd put a bit by every month once I'm earning, and take a night class to get comfortable with the computers, taught by a person. I'd also help run the union's out-of-work group, since people like Gerald need someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a worry sitting underneath. It's calmer, but I still have no money today and ten years is a long time to wait for something to feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do differently in year one, given you have ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't panic-apply to everything. I pick one path, the care certificate, and do it well. I'd also let myself learn the computer stuff slowly in a classroom, which I'd never do if the clock was two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust the people running things to share the gains. What would change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it written into law, with a union rep on the board, and then seeing it happen for ordinary people. Promises I've heard. I'd want a pension and a wage that doesn't fall because a machine does half the work.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if we use it to plan.
I'd ask for free courses, **public care jobs** and unions at the table.
think: Ten years lets me retrain and get a decent **care job**.
I still don't trust the people running things to **share the gains**.
do: Take the care certificate, then a **nursing assistant** course.
Save a little every month once I'm earning.
Help run the union's **out-of-work group** for people like Gerald.
feel: Hopeful, with a **worry** underneath, because I have no money today.
S4.quote: I don't panic-apply to everything. I pick one path, the care certificate, and do it well.
fieldNote: The long window moves her to **one path** instead of panic applications.
Trust is conditional: she wants rights in law, not promises.
Still anxious because the cushion is empty today.

steps.text: Complete the care certificate, then a nursing assistant course
Save a little every month once in work
Run the union's out-of-work group with older members like Gerald
Back a law that puts union reps on automation boards

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, no question. Two years is too short for someone with no savings and no plan, and I know how long it takes the benefits office to answer a letter. What would help is income support that's ready before the layoffs, a free course taught by a person, and a union in the room when decisions are made.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't stupid for not trusting the machines. I'm not against change, I just want to see who gains from it. I'd like someone to ask the people behind the glass before the glass comes down.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change, I just want to see who gains from it. I'd like someone to ask the people behind the glass before the glass comes down.
portrait: Uma is **34**, lives alone above a launderette with her cat, and is on **benefits only** with no savings.
She sold train tickets for **eleven years** until the office closed in June and now job hunts at the library.
She distrusts AI tools and online application boxes, and trusts **people and unions** more.
She blames employers who choose cheap over people, and moves from anxious to **panicked** as the warning time shrinks.
With more time she picks one path, a **care certificate**, and walks towards it slowly.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because two years is too little time with no savings and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** ready before layoffs, plus a free course taught by a person.
A **union** in the room when automation decisions are made.
